newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Markets keep watchful eye on Indonesian politics.
newsitem.headline: Markets keep watchful eye on Indonesian politics.

text.p: Financial markets are keeping a watchful eye on Indonesia's political process as the country gears up for general elections in May.

There is a consensus among political and economic analysts that the Indonesian economy, one of the tiger cubs of Asia, is in good shape, although the benefits of growth have still to reach the lower rungs of society.
"Generally speaking, the economy is in pretty good shape," Harry Tjan Silalahi, senior analyst at the independent Centre for Strategic and International Studies, told Reuters.

"Of course, political stability is a question. The general elections are in May, so the political temperature will climb up a bit because of that," he said. However, he was optimistic over the future, he said.

Analysts have blamed riots in the past few months in Java -- with over half of the country's 200 million population -- on socio-economic tensions, a distrust of the judiciary and anger at the level of corruption in the police and bureaucracy.

"Although the recent riots have not rattled the (stock) market, everyone is watching the political situation closely," Jos Parengkuan, research director at PT Lippo Securities, wrote in a recent column.

Another analyst questioned to what extent investors had factored political risk into the Jakarta stock market. The composite index has shot up from just over 560 points, when the capital was hit by its worst riots in two decades last July, to its current 700 level.

"While every country has a greater or lesser degree of political risk factored into the equities market, in Indonesia's case the expectation is currently that the elections will pass without any major disruptions," said the analyst, who asked not to be named
"Should there, in fact, be any kind of demonstrations on the streets...I think equity values will suffer."

Political analysts say there is no doubt the ruling Golkar party will win the May 29 elections, with the two legal minority parties -- the Moslem-oriented United Development Party (PPP) and the fractured Christian-National Indonesian Democratic Party (DPI) -- trailing far behind.
"In the larger scheme of things, we believe the upcoming election is essentially a non-event for two reasons," Parengkuan said in his column.
First, a Golkar victory was assured, with probably more votes than the 68 percent it took in the last elections in 1992.

"Second, this year's election affects only the parliament and not the presidency. The presidential election is not until...1998, and thus, no changes to the government nor to major economic policies are expected this year," Parengkuan said.
Analysts say the government has also taken a firm grip on the political process, moving to neutralise potential sources of opposition.

But there is a feeling that disturbances, especially in Jakarta where they could be easily filmed for television, would unsettle foreign investors in particular. Analysts note, however, that domestic investors are playing an increasing role in the market, tending to offset foreign jitters.
"There are some worrying signs about social tensions that need to be addressed. But I do not feel that the election itself will be turbulent," political analyst Dewi Fortuna Anwar told Reuters.
"The socio-ethnic conflicts (so far) are far removed. It's when the conflicts are in the capital itself that you have to look out," she said.
President Suharto, 75, who is widely expected to seek a seventh five-year term next year, has spoken of the disparities in wealth increasingly evident as the economy forges ahead.
"We can all witness the growth, but the problem now is that our economy's growth is dominated by a certain group," he was quoted as telling businessmen on Saturday.
"We must overcome this...because our development aims to give prosperity to as many people as possible."
